---
title: "API overview"
---

The extension registers the PHP module `phit` (`extension=phit`, Composer
`ext-phit`). Every function is in the `Phit` namespace and is named by prefix.

| Prefix or name | Purpose | Reference |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `fit_lm`, `fit_glm`, `fit_lmer`, `fit_glmer`, `model_matrix`, `predict` | Formula models and prediction | [Model formulas](formulas.qmd) |
| `fit_ols`, `fit_logistic`, `fit_probit`, `fit_poisson`, `fit_mixed_intercept`, `fit_mixed`, `fit_logistic_mixed` | Models on numeric matrices | [Matrix model functions](reference-models.qmd) |
| `dist_*` | Densities, CDFs, quantiles and seeded samples | [Distributions and utilities](reference-utilities.qmd) |
| `stat_*` | Descriptive statistics, kernel density, interpolation and the ECDF | [Distributions and utilities](reference-utilities.qmd) |
| `draws_*` | Weighted posterior-draw summaries and transforms | [Distributions and utilities](reference-utilities.qmd#posterior-draw-numerical-kernels) |
| `optimize`, `uniroot` | One-dimensional minimization and root finding | [Distributions and utilities](reference-utilities.qmd#one-dimensional-optimization-and-root-finding) |
| `permutation_rng` | Seeded permutations and samples without replacement | [Seeded sampling](rng.qmd) |
| `read_csv`, `CsvReader` | Reading delimited text files | [Reading CSV files](io.qmd) |

Import the functions you use:

```php
use function Phit\{fit_lm, predict, dist_normal_quantile};
```

`stubs/phit.php` in the repository declares every signature with PHPDoc array
shapes for IDEs and static analysis. Do not load it at runtime.

## PHP entry points

```php
Phit\fit_ols(array $x, array $y, string $missing = 'drop', ?array $weights = null, ?array $offset = null, bool $intercept = true): array;
Phit\fit_logistic(array $x, array $y, string $missing = 'drop', ?array $weights = null, ?array $offset = null, bool $intercept = true): array;
Phit\fit_probit(array $x, array $y, string $missing = 'drop', ?array $weights = null, ?array $offset = null, bool $intercept = true): array;
Phit\fit_poisson(array $x, array $y, string $missing = 'drop', ?array $weights = null, ?array $offset = null, bool $intercept = true): array;

// Formula interfaces over the same cores; $data is named columns or an object with toModelData()/toColumns().
Phit\model_matrix(string $formula, array|object $data, string $missing = 'drop'): array;
Phit\fit_lm(string $formula, array|object $data, string $missing = 'drop', array|string|null $weights = null): array;
Phit\fit_glm(string $formula, array|object $data, string $family = 'gaussian', string $link = '', string $missing = 'drop', array|string|null $weights = null): array;
Phit\fit_lmer(string $formula, array|object $data, bool $reml = true, string $missing = 'drop', array|string|null $weights = null, ...): array;
Phit\fit_glmer(string $formula, array|object $data, string $family = 'binomial', string $link = '', string $missing = 'drop', array|string|null $weights = null, ...): array;
```

All estimators are synchronous and stateless: each returns a complete fit without
retaining a model handle, input data or mutable configuration. It does not mutate
the caller's arrays. Repeated fits are independent.

## Formula interfaces

The formula functions parse an R model formula, build R's `model.matrix()` over
named columns, and call the estimation cores of `fit_ols`, `fit_logistic`,
`fit_probit`, `fit_poisson`, `fit_mixed`, and `fit_logistic_mixed`.
Each fit returns the complete result contract of its matrix function. It adds
`formula`, `response`, `columns` (coefficient names in coefficient order), `terms`,
`assign`, `intercept`, and `named` (`column => coefficient`). `fit_glm` and
`fit_glmer` also return `family` and `link`. `model_matrix` returns `y`,
`x` (including the `(Intercept)` column), the naming keys, `offset`, `random` designs
in the shape `fit_mixed` accepts, and the deletion accounting.

Missing-value deletion covers only the variables a formula uses, with the same
warning, `missing: 'raise'` behavior, and row accounting as the matrix functions.
`model_matrix` keeps unused factor levels, as `model.matrix()` does. The
fitting functions drop them, as `lm()`, `glm()`, and lme4 do. Unknown columns,
malformed factor descriptors, referenced list-columns, and invalid formulas raise
1001. Column-length mismatch raises 1002. Infinite transform results raise 1003.
Unsupported functions, families, links, and random-effect structures raise 1007.
Rank deficiency raises 1004. The [formula guide](formulas.qmd) defines the syntax,
contrasts, data shapes, verification, and every known difference from R.

## Fixed intercept {#fixed-intercept-convention-and-migration}

The seven matrix estimators take `bool $intercept = true`. Supply predictor columns only: the binding prepends an exact ones
column and the estimated intercept is coefficient 0, followed by predictors in
supplied column order. Covariance, standard errors, tests and intervals follow
that same order. Parameter counts and residual degrees of freedom include the
added coefficient. No input array is mutated.

`intercept: false` passes the supplied x matrix literally. It is both the opt-out
for a through-origin model and the compatibility option for callers already
supplying a complete design with ones. There is **no automatic detection** of
existing constant columns: leaving ones in x with the default creates a duplicate
intercept and a rank-deficiency error, rather than silently guessing intent.

For an intercept-only fit, supply one empty predictor row per outcome, such as
`x: array_fill(0, count($y), [])`. An empty sample or ragged matrix is still invalid;
empty predictor rows require `intercept: true`. Missing-row validation and deletion
still apply to outcomes, predictors, groups, weights and offsets before fitting.

The Rust core takes the design literally.

Random-effect designs `random[*].z` remain explicit; this option only constructs
the fixed design. For a random intercept/slope, z still needs `[1, slope]` rows.

## Errors and conversion

The binding accepts actual integers and floats as numeric elements, with null
and NAN representing missingness. PHP
integers are converted to f64, so integers beyond the exact range of double
precision may lose precision. Array keys and names do not label coefficients:
row order aligns x with y, and column order aligns all coefficient results.
Callers should normally supply packed lists and keep labels separately.

Missing values use listwise deletion by default, with one E_WARNING on a
successful fit that omits rows. missing: 'raise' rejects missingness. Values are
not coerced from strings, columns are not added, and aliased predictors are not
removed. fitted and residuals follow retained_rows order. See
[missing-data.qmd](missing-data.qmd) for validation order, warnings, accounting and
application handling. Applications can promote PHP warnings to exceptions.

Statistical and input failures use PHP Exception with stable numeric codes
1001–1008; see [the diagnostic/error contract](#v01-diagnostics-and-errors).
There are no estimator-specific exception classes. Callers can inspect getCode()
and should handle Throwable at their application boundary, since PHP argument
and runtime errors use their own types. Message text may change. If the extension is absent, the functions themselves are unavailable;
that is an installation failure rather than an invalid-data result.

NAN/INF are floating-point values in successful results, not failure sentinels.
Serialization helpers may map them to null using a documented policy, while the
native result preserves them. Current arithmetic uses f64; it is not arbitrary
precision, and extreme input scales can exceed its range.

## Rust boundary

```rust
pub fn fit_ols(
    x: Vec<Vec<f64>>,
    y: Vec<f64>,
) -> Result<OlsResult, StatsError>
```

The core owns its inputs and has no PHP dependency. OlsResult exposes the same
statistical fields as the PHP array (sample-deletion metadata is PHP-only), with Vec<f64> for numeric lists,
Vec<Vec<f64>> for covariance, Vec<[f64; 2]> for confidence intervals, f64 for
scalars, and usize for residual degrees of freedom. StatsError implements
Display and Error. The binding converts errors and values without implementing
statistical formulas.

See [design-philosophy.qmd](design-philosophy.qmd) for the boundary between this
raw API and optional convenience layers.

## Diagnostics and error codes {#v01-diagnostics-and-errors}

Every successful estimator returns `diagnostics`:

| Diagnostic key | Contract |
|---|---|
| converged | true on successful return, including direct OLS; failed fitting throws |
| solver | scaled_svd, newton_irls, fisher_scoring, profile_variance_search, bobyqa or nelder_mead |
| iterations, evaluations | Present only when the corresponding historical top-level key exists; same value, not a second counter |
| gradient_max | Present for logistic mixed only; same scaled-coordinate finite-difference score as its top-level key |
| boundary, singular | Present when the estimator already reports that flag; legitimate zero variance is permitted |
| warnings | list<string>; missing-row deletion, a reported near-singular covariance, or the logistic-mixed Laplace approximation advisory |

Warnings in this array are interpretation notices. Only listwise deletion also
emits the existing single PHP E_WARNING. Missing/undefined diagnostics are omitted;
there is no fabricated iteration count or universal score. General Gaussian
convergence still uses optimizer termination, parameter bounds, valid factors and
finite output; it does not have a final variance-parameter gradient/Hessian gate.
OLS has no iterative optimizer. Normal/Wald inference and local convergence do
not guarantee model adequacy or quadrature accuracy.

Statistical and input failures throw PHP `Exception` with a numeric `getCode()`:

| Code | Rust ErrorKind | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| 1001 | InvalidInput | Type/domain/control error, missing='raise', invalid groups/weights/counts |
| 1002 | DimensionMismatch | Shape/alignment or insufficient residual observations |
| 1003 | Nonfinite | Nonfinite values or arithmetic beyond floating-point range, including nonzero residual variance underflow |
| 1004 | RankDeficiency | Numerical design/information rank failure |
| 1005 | FactorizationFailure | Required linear solve or positive-definite information factor fails |
| 1006 | Nonconvergence | Budget/line-search/optimizer/score failure, separation or unsupported finite optimum at a search boundary |
| 1007 | Unsupported | Explicit size/count limit or unimplemented configuration |
| 1008 | Internal | Required decomposition output missing or an internal mathematical invariant fails |

Messages remain explanatory, not stable machine identifiers. Validation can
report the first failed check when multiple problems exist; combined validation
checks may use the most relevant category. Zend argument `TypeError`, result
conversion/runtime errors, and caught Rust panics are runtime errors rather
than statistical codes. Invalid data are checked before listwise deletion.
Rust `StatsError::new(kind, message)` carries the explicit enum without classifying
message text; `.0` remains the display message and `kind()` exposes its category.

Binomial calls limit trials to 1,000,000 per original row, and accepted
success-count rounding is canonicalized with `round(y*trials)/trials`.
For exact zero-variance OLS, the existing NaN/INF conventions remain; nonzero
variance underflow instead throws 1003. JSON consumers must handle documented
undefined OLS quantities explicitly; PHP's JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR rejects NaN/INF.
See the [v0.1 assessment](v0.1.qmd) for compatibility notes and tested stress ranges.
